name: Sofyan
desc: The simplest 4/4 usul, the building block of Ottoman classical and folk music, vocalized Düm Tek Te-ke (one düm and two teks). Two Sofyan cycles combine to form Düyek.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music); Turkish Music Portal usuls

name: Nim Sofyan
desc: A 2/4 usul, the shortest cycle, vocalized Düm Tek; the half-size of Sofyan and a basic unit of the larger composite usuls.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Semai
desc: A 3/4 usul vocalized Düm Tek Tek, used widely in saz semai instrumental forms; two Semai cycles or three Nim Sofyan form Yürük Semai.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Düyek
desc: An 8/8 usul, one of the most common cycles in Turkish music, vocalized Düm Tek-ke Düm Tek; effectively two Sofyan cycles joined. The backbone of many ilahis and oyun havaları.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; compmusic.upf.edu usul examples (https://compmusic.upf.edu/examples-usul-mmt)

name: Ağır Düyek
desc: The slow (ağır) variant of Düyek in 8/4 feel, giving each stroke greater weight and used in stately classical compositions and Mevlevi ceremonies.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Müsemmen
desc: An 8/8 aksak-feel usul grouped 3+2+3, giving a limping eight-beat cycle popular in folk and dance repertoire of Rumeli and the Aegean.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Devr-i Hindi
desc: A 7/8 usul grouped 2+2+3 (or 3+2+2), one of the classic aksak cycles of Ottoman art music, vocalized Düm Te-ke Tek Düm Tek.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Devr-i Turan
desc: A 7/8 usul grouped 3+2+2, a sibling of Devr-i Hindi with the long pulse placed first, used in classical and folk repertoire.
source: chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Türk Aksağı
desc: A 5/8 aksak usul grouped 2+3, vocalized Düm Tek Te-ek; two cycles combine to form Curcuna. Common in folk and classical song.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Aksak
desc: The classic 9/8 aksak usul grouped 2+2+2+3, the 'limping' meter of zeybek and oyun havası, vocalized Düm Te-ke Tek Te-ke Düm Tek-ke.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Ağır Aksak
desc: The slow form of the 9/8 aksak (2+2+2+3), giving a heavier, dignified gait used in art songs and şarkı; the same skeleton as Aksak performed at a stately tempo.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Karşılama
desc: The 9/8 Roman/Rumeli dance usul grouped 2+2+2+3, the lively karşılama 'greeting' face-to-face dance rhythm of Thrace, vocalized Düm Tek Düm Tek Düm Te-ke.
source: Oyun Havası, Melodigging; Donizetti Darbuka 9/8 aksak guide (https://www.donizettidarbuka.com/en/post/how-to-play-the-9-8-irregular-rhythm-on-the-darbuka-beginner-s-guide)

name: Roman 9/8
desc: The fast Turkish Romani (Roman havası) 9/8 grouped 2+2+2+3 with a syncopated düm on the off-pulse, the festive wedding groove of Roma clarinet and darbuka ensembles.
source: Darbuka Roman Havaları, Melodigging Oyun Havası; Roman havası darbuka references

name: Curcuna
desc: A 10/8 usul grouped 3+2+2+3 (two Türk Aksağı joined), vocalized Düm Tek Te-ke Düm Düm Tek Te-ke; the playful curcuna meter of köçekçe and oyun pieces.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; researchgate Yürük Semai–Curcuna study

name: Aksak Semai
desc: A 10/8 usul grouped 2+2+2+2+2, used in the aksak semai instrumental and beste forms of Ottoman classical music; vocalized Düm Tek Tek Tek Tek over five pulses.
source: chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Yürük Semai
desc: A 6/8 (6/4) usul grouped 3+3, vocalized Düm Tek Tek Düm Tek Tek; the flowing yürük ('walking') semai meter closing many fasıl suites, made of three Nim Sofyan.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia; researchgate Yürük Semai–Curcuna study

name: Sengin Semai
desc: A 6/4 usul, the 'weighty' semai grouped 3+3 at a slower, more ornamented tempo than Yürük Semai, common in classical şarkı.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Devr-i Kebir
desc: A grand 14/4 usul, one of the long classical cycles used in kâr, beste and Mevlevi ayin compositions; built from a sequence of düm and tek subgroups across fourteen beats.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Çenber
desc: A 24/4 classical usul ('the circle'), one of the great long cycles of Ottoman art music used in stately beste and kâr forms, here on a half-beat (eighth) grid.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Berefşan
desc: A 32/4 long classical usul (Berefşan/Berevşan), one of the extended cycles of Ottoman art music spanning thirty-two beats, used in monumental beste compositions.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Hafif
desc: A 32/4 classical usul whose name means 'light', a long compound cycle of Ottoman art music combining smaller usuls across thirty-two beats.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Sakîl
desc: A 48/4 monumental classical usul whose name means 'heavy', among the longest cycles of Ottoman art music; spans forty-eight beats here on a half-beat grid.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Remel
desc: A 28/4 long classical usul derived from the aruz poetic metre Remel, used in extended beste and kâr forms of Ottoman art music.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Fer'
desc: A 14/4 classical usul (Fer'), a medium-long cycle of Ottoman art music used in beste and ağır semai forms.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Çiftetelli
desc: The sensuous 8/8 (4/4) çiftetelli dance groove, vocalized Düm Tek Düm-Düm Tek, the undulating belly-dance and Roman rhythm of the eastern Mediterranean.
source: Oyun Havası, Melodigging; çiftetelli darbuka references

name: Mandıra
desc: A 9/8 usul grouped 2+2+2+3 used for the mandıra Roman dance, a relaxed swung cousin of karşılama played by Thracian Roma clarinet and darbuka ensembles.
source: Oyun Havası, Melodigging; Turkish 9/8 Roman dance references

name: Nim Devir
desc: A 6/4 usul ('half-cycle'), a shorter classical cycle related to the devir family, used in instrumental and vocal forms of Ottoman music.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Evfer
desc: A 9/8 usul grouped 2+2+2+3 widely used in Mevlevi and tekke music and ilahis, a devotional cousin of Aksak with a distinctive düm placement.
source: chromatone.center Turkish rhythms; Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia

name: Raksan
desc: A 15/8 usul ('dancing') grouped in additive subgroups, an aksak cycle used in lively classical and folk dance pieces.
source: chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Nim Evsat
desc: A 13/8 usul, an additive aksak cycle of Ottoman classical music ('half-Evsat'), used in instrumental and devotional repertoire.
source: chromatone.center Turkish rhythms (https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/turkish/)

name: Devr-i Revan
desc: A 14/8 usul ('flowing cycle') used in classical beste and kâr forms, a medium-long cycle with a gracefully moving düm-tek skeleton.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Nim Hafif
desc: A 16/4 classical usul ('half-Hafif'), a long composite cycle of Ottoman art music built from joined smaller usuls across sixteen beats.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Frenkçin
desc: A 12/8 classical usul of Ottoman art music, a medium cycle grouped in additive subgroups used in instrumental forms.
source: Rhythm in Turkish music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Turkish_music)

name: Reng
desc: The classic Persian 6/8 reng dance rhythm with a hemiola (6/8 + 3/4) feel, the most common metric cycle of Persian art music, played on tonbak with bass tom and rim baks.
source: Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/); Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia

name: Reng-e Chahar Mezrab
desc: The driving chahar mezrab ('four-pick') ostinato in 6/8, a fast virtuosic instrumental form of the dastgah where the tonbak fills the cycle with continuous rolling strokes.
source: Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Zarbi 2/4
desc: A Persian żarbī (metered) 2/4 cycle used in pishdaramad and reng, related to Arabic wahda; tonbak plays a low tom on the beat and rim accents off the beat.
source: Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia; Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Zarbi 4/4
desc: A Persian żarbī 4/4 cycle for pishdaramad and zarbi-avaz sections, with a steady bass tom and bright bak accents framing the metered melody.
source: Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Persian_music)

name: Persian 5/8
desc: A Persian 5/8 cycle grouped 2+3 (or 3+2), an asymmetric żarbī metre used in regional and art-music pieces, played on tonbak with tom and bak strokes.
source: Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Persian 7/8
desc: A Persian 7/8 cycle grouped 3+2+2 (or 2+2+3), an asymmetric metre of the żarbī repertoire, played on tonbak with a bass tom opening each subgroup.
source: Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Persian 10/8 Jorjina
desc: A Persian 10/8 cycle grouped 3+2+2+3, cognate with the Arabic jurjina, a lively asymmetric dance metre played on tonbak with paired bass toms framing the cycle.
source: Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Pishdaramad 6/4
desc: A stately 6/4 pishdaramad (overture) cycle of the dastgah, the slow metered prelude that opens a Persian classical suite, played on tonbak with broad toms and bak ornaments.
source: Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia; Persian Rhythms, Oud for Guitarists (https://www.oudforguitarists.com/persian-rhythms/)

name: Zarb-e Osul
desc: Zarb-e osul, the foundational metric cycle taught in the tonbak radif, an 8-beat żarbī pattern of tom and bak strokes underpinning composed sections of the dastgah.
source: Rhythmic forms in Persian art music, ResearchGate; Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia

name: Tasnif 6/8
desc: A 6/8 tasnif (ballad/song) accompaniment of Persian classical music, gentler than reng, where the tonbak supports a sung melody with rolling tom-bak figures.
source: Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Persian_music)

name: Azerbaijani Mugham Reng
desc: The lively 6/8 reng/diringi dance section of an Azerbaijani mugham, where naghara and daf drive a hemiola groove between the slow improvised mugham movements.
source: Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia; Azerbaijani mugham references

name: Heyrati
desc: Heyrati, a march-like metered zarbi-mugham rhythm of Azerbaijan in duple time, played on naghara with a firm bass and crisp rim accents under a fixed-tempo mugham.
source: Azerbaijani zarbi-mugham references; Rhythm in Persian music, Wikipedia

name: Doira Ufar
desc: Ufar, the fast 6/8 dance usul that closes each Shashmaqom suite, played on doira with deep bum (center) and sharp bak (rim) strokes driving an exuberant dance.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org (https://ppublishing.org/archive/publication/1050-uzbek-classical-music-and-rhythm-usul); Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Doira Samoî
desc: Samoî (Samoiy), a flowing 6/8 usul of the Shashmaqom instrumental cycle, with bum strokes opening each pulse group and bak strokes filling the dance-like motion.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashmaqam)

name: Doira Talqin
desc: Talqin (Talkin), a stately 7/8 usul of the Shashmaqom vocal cycle, where the doira's bum-bak pattern carries a measured, declamatory song section.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Doira Mukhammas
desc: Mukhammas ('fivefold'), a long instrumental usul of the Shashmaqom, one of the great composed cycles for doira accompaniment with a rich bum-bak architecture.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashmaqam)

name: Doira Sakil
desc: Sakil, a weighty long usul of the Shashmaqom instrumental repertoire, among the most extended doira cycles, building a grand procession of bum and bak strokes.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Doira Gardun
desc: Gardun, a duple instrumental usul of the Shashmaqom ('the wheel/heaven'), a steady doira cycle of alternating bum and bak that introduces many maqom movements.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashmaqam)

name: Doira Sarakhbor
desc: Sarakhbor, the grand opening vocal usul of a Shashmaqom maqom, a measured cycle whose doira pattern frames the highest sung climax of the suite.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Doira Savt
desc: Savt, a lyrical vocal usul of the Shashmaqom song cycle, where the doira supports an ornamented melody with a gently swung bum-bak figure.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Doira Chapandoz
desc: Chapandoz, an energetic Uzbek-Tajik dance usul evoking the horseback buzkashi rider, with a galloping doira pattern of alternating bum and bak strokes.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Doira traditional rhythm references

name: Doira Zang
desc: Zang, an asymmetric 5/8 (2+3) folk dance usul of the doira repertoire of the Ferghana and Tashkent traditions, with a limping bum-bak gait.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Doira traditional rhythm references

name: Doira Sarbakhsh
desc: Sarbakhsh, an introductory instrumental usul of the Tajik-Uzbek maqom tradition, a steady additive doira cycle that sets the meter before the main movement.
source: Uzbek classical music and rhythm (usul), ppublishing.org; Shashmaqam, Wikipedia

name: Uyghur Muqam Marghul
desc: A 7/8 marghul dance rhythm from the Uyghur On Ikki Muqam, where dap (frame drum) and naghra accelerate the suite's closing dastan and mäshräp dance sections.
source: Uyghur On Ikki Muqam, Wikipedia; Central Asian muqam rhythm references

name: Uyghur Muqam Sama
desc: The 7/8 sama dance rhythm of the Uyghur muqam, a communal circle-dance metre grouped 2+2+3 led by the dap frame drum at the climax of the suite.
source: Uyghur On Ikki Muqam, Wikipedia; Central Asian muqam rhythm references

name: Lazgi
desc: Lazgi, the exuberant Khorezm dance rhythm of Uzbekistan in a 6/8 hemiola feel, accelerating across the dance with driving doira bum and bak strokes.
source: Khorezm Lazgi (UNESCO ICH); Doira traditional rhythm references
